drills.label: Cold open
drills.question_line: SAM: Here's the first item. An insurer runs a three-step claims pipeline: classify the incoming claim
drills.answer_line: SAM: Back to the cold open. The claims pipeline on the top tier with thinking on
drills.stem: An insurer's three-step claims pipeline (classify, summarise documents, compose an adjuster note) runs every step on the top tier with extended thinking on. Monthly cost is 5x budget and median latency is past target. What should the architect do first?

options.A: Move every step to the smallest tier
options.B: Build an eval set per step, set pass thresholds in advance, move each step to the lowest tier that passes
options.C: Keep the top tier and truncate the supporting documents to cut input tokens
options.D: Fine-tune a smaller model on the top tier's outputs

drills.why: Measure before moving: per-step evals with thresholds set first. A downgrades without evidence, C drops evidence the adjuster needs, D jumps to fine-tuning.

drills.label: Drill
drills.question_line: SAM: Pause here and answer before we go on. A retail bank's support router sorts incoming messages into one
drills.answer_line: SAM: Correct. A router that needs no reasoning gains nothing from a thinking pass
drills.stem: A retail bank's support router sorts messages into one of six queues, on a mid tier with extended thinking enabled. Accuracy meets the target, but the router adds noticeable latency to every conversation. What's the best change?

options.A: Move the router to the top tier so it finishes its reasoning faster
options.B: Disable extended thinking and confirm on the eval set that accuracy holds
options.C: Add three worked examples per queue to the prompt
options.D: Cache the router's responses for a day

drills.why: A router that needs no reasoning gains nothing from a thinking pass but pays its latency and cost every request. Confirm on the eval: config changes are behaviour changes.

drills.label: Drill
drills.question_line: SAM: Pause here and answer before we go on. This one is choose two. A field-service company's ticket triage prompt
drills.answer_line: SAM: The answer is A and B. The rubric defines severity by impact
drills.scenario: Ticket triage priority swayed by tone
drills.stem: A field-service company's ticket triage prompt assigns priority by business impact. Angrily worded feature requests keep getting top priority. Which two changes address the root cause?

options.A: Add a few-shot example of an urgently worded feature request correctly given the lowest priority
options.B: Add an explicit rubric instruction to judge priority by impact and ignore tone
options.C: Move the prompt to a larger model tier
options.E: Add a dashboard tracking the distribution of priorities each day

drills.why: The rubric never says to ignore tone, so B closes that gap; the judgment is easier to show than describe, so A gives the counter-case. E is detective and fixes nothing.

drills.label: Drill
drills.question_line: SAM: Pause here and answer before we go on. A field-service assistant builds every request as follows
drills.answer_line: ALEX: B. The timestamp changes on every call, so the prefix never matches.
drills.stem: A field-service assistant builds each request: current timestamp and technician ID, then a 6,000-token equipment manual and safety rules, then the question. Calls arrive every few seconds. Caching is enabled, but the cache-read token count is always zero. What's the best fix?

options.B: Move the timestamp and technician ID after the manual and safety rules so the fixed block is the prefix
options.C: Switch to a smaller model tier
options.D: Summarise the manual down to 500 tokens

drills.why: The timestamp changes on every call, so the prefix never matches. Reorder, then confirm hits in the usage field. D is the blunt cut that discards safety content.

drills.prompt: Name the five task statements this episode covered, or the giveaway for each.

Route tiers by step or input class, each choice backed by an eval

Underspecification: the model fills silent gaps differently each run
Guardrails belong in the output contract, not just role text
A system prompt is not enforcement: add runtime controls

Few-shot: format or judgment easier to show than describe
Chain-of-thought: when the reasoning path decides the answer
The lightest technique that meets the requirement
What ships is the prompt and model pairing
Bias shows in aggregate: neutral phrasing, balanced examples
Context windows and tokens: Context window, retrieval, application state, memory: keep them apart
The window is a ceiling, not a target; measure tokens
Too large: rejected; output hits the ceiling: truncated
Progressive is the production default; monolithic for bounded tasks
Model the token distribution, not the average
Prompt reuse and caching: The cache matches a stable prefix: tools, then system, then messages
Static before dynamic, breakpoint at the boundary
Explicit cache control: writes cost more, reads a fraction
5-minute default lifetime; verify hits in the usage field
Truncation is blind; caching keeps required content
Skill: a versioned SKILL.md unit for procedures shared across teams
Five to remember: Start on Sonnet; move up or down only on eval evidence, threshold set before the run
Lightest technique: zero-shot by default, few-shot to show, chain-of-thought when the path decides
Guardrails in the output contract and runtime controls, not just role text
The window is a ceiling: default progressive, combine strategies by phase, model the token tail
Static before dynamic: verify cache hits in the usage field; Skills for versioned, shared procedures
Recap: the exam tells: Stronger tier with no measurement named → bigger-model distractor
Accuracy meets the target and thinking is on → turn it off, confirm on the eval
Fine-tuning, with no failed prompt work in the stem → out of order
"Must never" or "guarantee" → structure in the output contract, not a firmer sentence
Easier to show → few-shot; path decides the answer → chain-of-thought; otherwise zero-shot
Cost climbs turn after turn, or rests on the average → progressive context and the token tail
Caching on, cache-read count zero → something volatile before the fixed block
Required fixed block with a cost or latency complaint → caching, never truncation; drifting copies → Skill
